MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN TORONTO "GLOBE AND MAIL"
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, arising out of an editorial in the Toronto Globe and Mail in which the editorial writer has made a personal attack on me in connection with the discharge of my duties in this house last week. I should make it plain at the outset that I have no objection to the cartoon above the editorial. I recognize the figure, if not the face.
The editorial itself is the type of attack that I think any member should take objection to because, first, it is highly prejudicial; and second, it makes allegations which are unsupported by the facts and indeed insulting to me.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN TORONTO "GLOBE AND MAIL"
speechtext: You ought to hear what I think about you.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN TORONTO "GLOBE AND MAIL"
speechtext: I have many opportunities of hearing the hon. member, and I am not always so sure that they are welcome.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN TORONTO "GLOBE AND MAIL"
speechtext: I am changing my mind about capital punishment.

subtopic: MR. NUGENT    REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN TORONTO "GLOBE AND MAIL"
speechtext:
The particular line to which I take objection is the one that says my action was taken in defence of no principles. I feel that the story on the front page of the same paper, if the editorial writer had bothered to familiarize himself with that even without bothering to read Hansard, would have informed the writer that the charges were not supported. The principles involved, as any member of this house would recognize, were very clearly stated. They were that the government is not mightier than parliament. There are others; that no government can get away with trying to use a club on parliament; that individual members in this house have a responsibility which they must discharge as their conscience dictates, no matter how unpopular that might make them; that co-operation of parliament and government is not a one way street.
I think the editorial writer, if he will bother to read Hansard the next time, will realize that if he is incapable of being fair he should at least try to be accurate.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, arising out of the terrible catastrophe that struck Alaska just before the week end and also brought serious damage to Vancouver island and other parts of the Pacific coast, I would ask the Prime Minister whether any request has been received from the province of British Columbia for the country as a whole to assist in the serious losses suffered by the people in the areas in B.C. that were affected.
At the same time I want to say to the Prime Minister that we join with him in the message of sympathy that was extended to the United States on the terrible catastrophe that took place.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has been appointed by the government to co-ordinate the activities of the federal government with a view to assisting the province of British Columbia and the area concerned in the tragic damage that area has suffered. Perhaps, if the right hon. gentleman agrees, I might ask my colleague to make a report on what has been done.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was in Vancouver on Friday night, and early Saturday morning I had a communication from the Prime Minister's office asking me to contact Premier Bennett with an offer of federal assistance if the extent of the damage was beyond the capacity of the municipalities and the province to carry.
I endeavoured to contact Premier Bennett, without avail; then Attorney General Bonner; then Hon. Mr. Kiernan, and finally I spoke to Hon. Leslie Peterson, the provincial minister of labour. I informed him of this offer and he told me that quite probably investigations were already under way but, if not, he would see they would be undertaken at once and he would reply. We have not heard anything yet, and to this moment the government of Canada has not had an application for assistance from the government of the province of British Columbia.

Inquiries of the Ministry
I might add that we have had requests for assistance from the mayors of the two cities of Port Alberni and Alberni, and latterly a second request for the use of army engineers stationed at Chilliwack. Our reply to them has been that we would be glad to give such aid and assistance, and indeed lend personnel, if the request comes from the government of the province of British Columbia. I want to assure the right hon. gentleman that the Department of National Defence has been working very closely with us on this, and is quite prepared to act upon a moment's notice. Also the emergency measures organization, the Red Cross and other agencies in the province of British Columbia are either working effectively now or are prepared to act on a moment's notice if they are required.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext: I thank the hon. gentleman. As I see it the matter now rests with the government of the province of British Columbia to request assistance in the event that the damage was such as to constitute a national disaster. I would also like to ask the Prime Minister whether, with a view to showing Canada's general attitude, a contribution will be made to the Red Cross for use in the devastated areas of Alaska.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext: In our message to the President, to which the right hon. gentleman referred a moment ago, we have indicated not only our sympathy for the victims of the disaster but our desire to assist if assistance is called for, and we have intimated to the President that we are making preparatory arrangements in the event that such a request should be made. May I say that I would be very glad to take up with the Red Cross, apart from this message to the President of the United States, the possibility of assisting the Canadian Red Cross if their help is required by the agencies concerned.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext:
I should like to ask a related question on the subject, but first, perhaps, as the member representing the constituency which has suffered the damage, might I be permitted to express my appreciation of the offer which has been made by the Prime Minister and the government to provide assistance should the province request it.
I should like to direct my related question to the Minister of Public Works and ask whether he or his department has yet received any report as to the damage which may have been sustained by federal harbour installations along the west coast of Vancouver island; and, if damage has occurred, whether measures are being proceeded with to effect a speedy repair of the installations in ques-

tion which are, of course, of great concern to the fishing fleet and other users along the west coast.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. P. Deschaieleis (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext: We are looking into this matter at the moment. I have no special information to give the hon. member at the present time, but officials of my department are looking into the matter.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I put a supplementary question?
Is the Prime Minister aware of the report to the effect that an atomic explosion in the Pacific caused the disaster last Friday in Alaska and in British Columbia, and that an investigation is being held in that connection? [Text]

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext: No, I am not aware of those rumours, but I am aware of the scientific information which has already appeared and which indicates that it was an earthquake. [Translation]

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does the Prime Minister recognize that an earthquake can be caused by an atomic explosion.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext:
May I ask the
Prime Minister if his attention has been called to an article in today's Gazette which states that Mr. Dan Campbell intends to ask the department of municipal affairs that Port Alberni and Alberni be called a disaster area, and that a committee of some kind is being set up to investigate the matter?

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO ASSISTANCE TO B.C. AND ALASKA
speechtext: Yes, I saw that report. It indicates that the provincial government is looking into the matter and, as already stated, if the provincial government, having declared this a disaster area, require federal assistance they will receive federal assistance.

When I raised the question Thursday last, the minister replied that he was not aware of such a situation.
Well, we have in the house representatives of every Canadian party and every time a member raises a question the government turns a deaf ear. I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to instruct his officials to listen or consider carefully what the members say in the house, because when we raise a question, it is not only because we like to speak, but because our constituents are asking us to intervene.
With regard to the point I am raising now, the farmers say that they have not seen such prices since the 1929 depression; the minister tells us that this is a regional problem. Well, Mr. Chairman, it is not a regional problem and, to prove it, I have here a letter from a farmer, Mr. Josephat Jolin, from Amos, in Abitibi. It was published in La Terre de Chez Nous on February 12, 1964, and reads as follows:
I am writing you to ask on behalf of all farmers if it would not be possible to add market prices for cow hides.
Last February 14, X went to Amos, in Abitibi, with a cow's hide in perfect condition, without any knife cut, well salted, weighing 60 lbs. and I get $1.50 for it. For a calf's skin weighing 12 lbs., also in perfect condition, 50 cents.
I see that Liberal members are making fun of my remarks. As a matter of fact, the province of Quebec is represented by 46 Liberal members in the house and not one of them saw fit to raise that question and to make suggestions to the Department of Agriculture. They have failed in their duty and instead of laughing at the remarks we make in this house, they should help the farmers. They should rise and point out to the Minister of Agriculture the problems prevailing not only in our province but throughout Canada.

I shall proceed with the reading of this letter for the information of the Minister of Agriculture.
We feel this is unreasonable and that is why I think we would be in a better position to defend ourselves if we received market prices.
Well, Mr. Chairman, the problem is not only regional; it is nation-wide. If the price for calf hides, which was 42.Y cents per pound last year, is down to 7 cents a pound this year, it means that the price of meat to the consumer increases and the consumer has to pay 10, 15 and even 20 cents more per pound for the meat purchased from the butcher.
I raise this question once again and I ask the Minister of Agriculture to give it careful consideration because, believe me, Mr. Chairman, this constitutes a loss of $10 to $12 million a year for Canadian farmers.
I now want briefly to come back to the matter of feed grain. Last Thursday, for instance, the minister told us:
I do not have the latest figures at hand, but between mid-October and mid-March, there has been no significant change in prices.
Well, as far as feed grain is concerned, the Liberal party since the last election, did not keep the formal promises it made to every Canadian, and more particularly to the province of Quebec. Those promises had been made by an official spokesman of the party on the national television network, and anybody can still read them in an editorial published in La Terre de Chez Nous, under the headings:
Beware of Mr. Pearson's figure skating. Our farming industry is on the auction block in Ottawa.
The price of feed grain has increased by 30 cents a hundredweight between October and February, which means $6 a ton. This is hardly what we would call a stable price.
We want the government to take a decision at last. It is true that when the government decided to pay for storage at a cost of $1 million per year, there was some improvement; but, even if credit is given to the Minister of Agriculture for that improvement, it is still inadequate, and an efficient policy should be set up at the earliest possible date, so that we might say to the eastern farmers in Canada: "We are looking after your problems and we did find a solution to the feed grain problem".
The minister also discussed farm credit. On that matter, he said: "Some people claim we have not done much in that field." And here I quoted the minister.
If it had not been for the improved farm credit legislation introduced by the previous government, without the wonderful efficiency of the Farm Credit Corporation officials, how could the minister tell us there were loans made in 1963?

Surely, he cannot take the credit for that legislation, since no amendment was made. What we are asking for is an improvement of the act, instead of being told: "We have done something in that field." We want the minister to give us immediately his program and his views on the improvements to be made to the federal Farm Credit Act.
Since the hon. gentlemen opposite took office, that is since April 8, 1963, what have they done for farming in Canada? What have those same people done who, during the election campaign, said they were going to improve the farmer's lot? Where are the promises they made all across the country during weeks and weeks?
Where do our hon. friends stand with the crop insurance legislation, which was passed by a Conservative government and which they, the Liberals, were to improve in order to bring it more in line with the agreements concluded with the provinces? What progress has been made in the negotiation concerning crop insurance, a measure to be promulgated by the provinces of Canada?
Mr. Chairman, we could also ask the gov-vernment what progress has been made in the negotiations with the provinces concerning the adoption of a school milk program which we heard so much about, for such a long time, when the hon. gentlemen were sitting on this side of the house? However, not a single word was said about that matter up to the present.
Mr. Chairman, where are the improvements promised by this government to Canadian farmers, and especially to those of eastern Canada as far as dairy products are concerned? I have said time and time again in this house that while the price of milk in the province of Quebec last year was lower than in 1962, it should have been from 20 to 25 cents higher per 100 pounds, because the price of dairy products, including cheese, was higher on the market, thanks to the policies advocated by the Conservative government when it was in office. What progress has been made in the talks between the provinces and the dairy farmers with respect to the setting up of a dairy industry board?
Mr. Chairman, those are questions to which we should like to get answers, and it is certainly not by standing up and using phrases like "a lot of junk" or something like that, that answers can be given to sensible questions emanating not from us but from the farmers who submit them to us, so that we may find a solution to the agricultural problem.

Mr. Chairman, we are sitting
here on Monday, March 30, a day when most of us would much prefer to be home, and I am sure that if the government had wanted to manage the affairs of this country in a reasonable manner we should have been home.
Order.

I am speaking on agriculture and on the first item of the supplementary estimates, and I am about to inform the arrogant hon. gentlemen opposite that we still have not received the information for which we asked.
When this time first came up we asked that it stand because there were several matters which we, as responsible members of parliament, felt were important and had been left unexplained. There were grave doubts as to the legality of actions taken by the government between February 3 and February 20. We said that as members of parliament we could hardly be content to put our stamp of approval on what had been done when those actions might have been taken illegally. Money might have been spent illegally, and we as members of the committee might have been placed in the position of approving those improper expenditures.
It was not until last Thursday that we were finally given any statement on this matter. The Minister of Transport then read a statement by the Prime Minister touching lightly on the question. I use those words advisedly because the statement read by the Minister of Transport was circuitous, evasive, vague. The committee had asked that these items be allowed to stand because we were disturbed by the possibility of illegalities, and when we asked for a firm statement on the government's position the attitude we took was reasonable. We had stressed that the committee should not be asked to pass lightly over such questions as the legality or illegality of government action.

We did not go too deeply into certain other questions, though I am sure these aspects must have disturbed the public as much as they disturbed members of this house; namely, why there was such dissension within the cabinet to lead to such confusion; whether there was a battle going on within the cabinet; what was the effect of these orders in council, and how lightly must the government itself regard these orders if it could pass them, give them the effect of law, and then ignore them completely.
All the government has given us is this one vague statement, and I do not think the committee should be expected to content itself with an answer which takes refuge in technicalities despite the fact that a minister of the crown has signed agreements when he had no authority whatsoever to do so. For an opposition to condone such action would constitute a complete abandonment of its responsibilities.
I know that as late as the middle of March people in charge of the farm credit organization, the ARDA program, the P.F.R.A. program and so on were not sure who was the responsible minister. Perhaps it was unfair to ask them who was the responsible minister. Perhaps they felt that no matter who was the minister in charge, he was not responsible. I know that many telephone calls were made in an attempt to get a straight answer, in an effort to be sure which minister was responsible for those sections. But the people concerned did not know, and this was later than March 5.
To review briefly the actions of the government, an order in council passed on February 3 was revoked on February 20 and another order in council dealing with only some of those sections was made on March 15. Perhaps it was unfair to telephone as late as March 15 and ask who was the responsible minister because, judging from past experience, the government might have intended to revoke the order of March 5 or, in its own words, decide not to proceed with it. Certainly the answers given by the people working in those sections indicated that they were not sure whether the government knew what it was going to do.
I suggest it is part of the duty of members of this committee to seek from the government some information as to the morale of those engaged in the sections of the department affected by this classic example of administrative bungling. For a long time, I suggest, those sections had been operating, and operating very well, under a strong and competent minister during the life of the previous government. They knew what they were doing. They had a minister who took responsibility, who gave them guidance and made sure
Supply-Agriculture
that those programs operated and operated well. They have now been subject to what appear to have been weeks of wrangling. We have not even been given any firm statement by the government to reassure us that those weeks of wrangling are past. I suggest that if it is necessary to have a minister, if it is helpful to have a minister, then the department should be able to rely on getting some guidance from him. It is a pretty tough situation when they do not even know whether or not they have a minister.
I think we would like to see answered those two notices of motion for production of papers brought forward by the hon. member for Provencher. The statement read the other day by the Minister of Transport treats the whole question too lightly as to what went on. We are aware, at least, of the eight ARDA agreements which, according to the information given us in this house, are not now in effect at all. My leader gave a very strong hint to the government that we would cooperate; that the least we should see is remedial, retroactive legislation to make sure that these items are covered; that we on this side of the house will co-operate and see that is done, and we had not one word from the government on that matter.
I am sure that some hon. members feel we are perhaps taking a rather long time on this item. If we are, it is because we do not get any answers. I suggest that this is anything but lack of co-operation on our part. We do regard these matters as serious. We think there is a serious legal problem. The suggestion made by the Minister of Transport that he will have the Minister of Forestry sign these agreements indicates some realization on the government benches that there is a legal problem; and what we have suggested is that we will co-operate to help the government get over it. We just want a little frankness from the government. We want to know exactly what was done. We want them to initiate some step to make sure that this matter is corrected.
If this is being very stubborn, Mr. Chairman, then I submit I am being very stubborn. I may be old fashioned, but I would like to see government business properly and legally done. I would like to see the government come to parliament, not with a club in their hands saying "You will do this or else", but come to parliament and say "All right; we made a mistake. We want it fixed. This is what we would like done. Will you co-operate?" When we see this sort of action, we will co-operate. So long as the government is going to sit on its hands and say "Take it as is, and we couldn't care less how it is", then they are liable to find us being a little stubborn.

I do hope that before it is attempted to pass this item some member of the government will rise and give us a responsible answer to these questions; that they will give some reasonable satisfaction to this house, so that the business of this country can be straightened out, these questions can be answered, and we can properly pass this item.

Mr. Chairman, we hear
many declarations of love and speeches on the Canadian farmer's lot. A few moments ago, the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) dealt with the needs of our eastern farmers of which we are all aware. Those urgent problems, he said, are yet unsolved, and the government seems unwilling to provide a solution.
When my good friend was a member of the government, the same conditions prevailed. And they still prevail today. The statements made in this house are not so much meant to help the farmer as to draw the attention of Hansard readers. That is the main object of all those fond declarations and speeches. Farming is not considered an essential or basic Canadian industry. No, the farmer is just a football; for instance, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) just stated that this government does nothing for the farmers, though he knows very well that this government sold more wheat to the communists all over the world than even the Conservatives did. He must be aware of the fact. When the Conservatives were selling wheat to the Chinese and Russian communists, they were condemned by the Liberals. Today, the Conservatives are blaming the Liberals for selling more wheat than they ever did to those countries.
Mr. Chairman, all those statements and declarations meant for the farmer, in no way take into account that agriculture is, after all, Canada's basic industry. If that basic industry is not organized, if neither prosperous nor stable, it will be impossible to stop this nation from disintegrating entirely, and its economy from collapsing.
Quite recently, there were reports from Soviet Russia regarding the handing over of some land to private enterprise, because the government made a mess of the whole business when it meddled with farming in that country.
Now, we do not want the state to administer our farming industry, but we want our farmers to get some help from the government so that they would prosper and attain a higher standard of living than at present, because they are certainly struggling with a system that has become intolerable.

Mr. Chairman, we have reached a point where farmers have to emigrate to cities, abandon their land and seek outside work to support their families. In the face of such a situation we ask ourselves where agriculture is going, where the farmer himself is going?
Mr. Chairman, reforms have to be made. There is above all assistance to be granted farmers in eastern Canada. For instance, if we consider that farmers in western Canada earn more than $6,500 per year, whereas, in the province of Quebec, most farmers do not earn more than $2,000 a year, we may wonder what will be the fate of farmers, of those people who rise at four or five o'clock in the morning to milk their cows and who go to bed at ten or eleven o'clock at night. For what do these people work? For 5 or 6 cents per hour, whereas there are people who spend their time speaking in favour of farmers and who rise at ten o'clock in the morning to milk the farmers instead of the cows.
Mr. Chairman, the farmers in eastern Canada need assistance.
Order.

Why, for instance, when the Conservatives were in power-
I see my hon. friend from Pontiac-Temis-camingue (Mr. Martineau), in the corner of the house, over there, trying to interrupt me. What was done for farmers in his own constituency when the Conservatives were in power? What was done in Temiscamingue, a constituency with which I am very familiar?

Mr. Chairman, I would ask the hon. member to read again what he said, as recorded in Hansard, and he will see that he charged the present government with failure to face its obligations in the case of Canadian farmers.
Having said this, I was asserting that our farmers have to take outside work to be in a position to keep their farms, that there is an exodus of farmers towards the cities, that the Canadian agricultural policy no longer meets the needs of the farmers.
In view of the large sales of wheat to some communist countries, no doubt western farmers have earned an interesting income. In this respect, the farmers, regardless of the party in power, directly benefited from these important sales of wheat to other countries.
On various occasions, I called the attention of the house to this point: why should not the government set up or prepare a policy to enable eastern farmers, for instance, to buy feed grain or wheat produced in western Canada at the same price we sell those products to foreign countries?
Surely, if we can be generous to foreign countries, we ought to do the same for our own farmers. When we travel through farming communities, in the south of the province of Quebec, where in some cases, seven, eight, nine and even ten generations succeeded each other on the same farm, we readily realize that it is not because our farmers lacked courage or good will that after seven, eight or nine generations of hard labour, today's farmer is involved with provincial or federal farm credit.
Why are our farmers faced with such a situation?
Let us take a look at the settlement areas where an attempt was made to place settlers and favour farming. In those regions, 20 or 25 years ago, there were settlements of 200 or 250 families, but today, after 20 or 25 years of existence, there are only 80 or 85 families left, the others having gone back to the city looking for means to make a living and get
Supply-Agriculture
a decent salary. And eventually, when there is not enough work, people become unemployed and have to depend on the government, the Department of Labour or the unemployment insurance commission.
To avoid that disaster for agriculture, why is not agriculture organized on a solid basis through assistance, for instance, to the establishment of farmers' sons who today, are not interested in staying on the family farm? Why not assist in the consolidation of old farms? Why not assist rural planning all across the province and the country, but especially in eastern Canada, where the problem is most acute and most urgent?
We must be assured that a farm policy is being developed, and that no advantages are taken away from an area to be given to another one, when both need help.
It is certainly possible to create a market in the province of Quebec. The government could guarantee the sale of food products and so on, help the construction of cold storages, in short help agriculture in eastern Canada as it does in western Canada.
The products of eastern Canada are as much in demand throughout the world as wheat. We should organize the agricultural production of eastern Canada and its exportation to southern countries. There are tremendous possibilities along those lines.
A short time ago, I met a man dealing in imports and exports, he gave me the inside story of what is happening today in the field of butter production and marketing. He suggested it might be interesting by using the means we have in this country, to put butter in small three ounce cans and sell it to southern countries which are interested in buying butter packed that way. The Minister of Agriculture was made aware of that. And do you know what the answer was? It was said that we could not do it, since we are not allowed to pack our butter in a different way; it was added however that industry is organizing such a marketing of Canadian butter, which would be exported to Germany where it would be packed in boxes and resold on the world markets. The Minister of Agriculture is well aware of that.
We might have created instead a new industry in the Granby area for instance, an industry that would have employed 2,000 or 3,000 men, while these 2,000 or 3,000 people will be Germans working in Germany to pack butter coming from Canada. Why? Because there are financial interests to be protected in the field of exportation and importation. The Minister of Agriculture is also aware of that.
We cannot make decisions by ourselves in Canada. We are afraid of assuming responsibilities, but we dare proclaim in this house

our love for the Canadian farmer, butter manufacturer or dairy producer, and so on.
Mr. Chairman, agriculture is an important item in a country. I said at the beginning that this industry is the very basis of a stable economy. If we are to have a stable economy- because without it all other social classes could not exist-we all depend on agriculture, because there we take the source of life, there we maintain the way of life that we have at the present time in this country.
We cannot be satisfied with making speeches, paying lip service to agriculture and doing nothing to help the farmers.
I do not come from a specifically agricultural area myself. True, we do have a bit of farming in our settlements, but I am from a mining region. On the other hand, the riding next to mine, which I represented in the House of Commons from 1946 to 1949, that is the constituency of Pontiac-Temiscamingue, is essentially agricultural. It is one of the most beautiful agricultural ridings in the whole province of Quebec. Now, that constituency has a problem concerning the settlement of farmers' sons and also one of consolidation to allow farmers to sell their products normally. There is an abundance of products, but nobody knows what to do with them.
And, with all that abundance, millions of dollars are giving rise to heated discussions; commissions are being set up to hold inquiries designed to set up more commissions; money is being provided to replenish the funds of the agricultural products board; salvage operations are being conducted right and left, with the result that the only one not being rescued is the farmer, who keeps on paying taxes and being overtaxed but does not manage to sell his products. And all the while we are keeping afloat a whole bunch of bureaucrats throughout Canada at the farmers' expense.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take more of the committee's time. Only, let us stop making speeches and referring constantly to the magnificent role played by the farmers of the province and of Canada as a whole, when we do not even have the courage to put forward legislation to assist Canadian farmers, while we provide millions of dollars for all sorts of other things but cannot even find the time, for instance, to think of organizing a stable agriculture which would give Canada a look completely different from the one it has now.
Mr. Chairman, the farmers need our help, they certainly do. They need our attention. Of all the classes in our society, they get the least recognition and the worst treatment all across Canada wherever you go. They may be better treated in western Canada-which is essentially a farming area-than in eastern Canada; all you have to do is to visit the

agricultural parishes and the farmers themselves to see that this is true. You cannot get a true picture by driving 60 or 90 miles an hour past well painted farm buildings; indeed not.
Let us go right into the farmer's home to inquire on the spot about the conditions prevailing in our province. Then, I trust that the Minister of Agriculture will assume his responsibilities with regard to the Canadian public, and introduce some legislation meeting with the approval not only of a single group, or of all hon. members, but of the whole Canadian people, because no social class, I am certain, has yet been treated as unfairly as the farmers.
Let us stop being facetious and let us try to serve them better in future.

Mr. Chairman, I think there is more interest across Canada at this time in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture than at any other time when agricultural estimates have been brought before the house. Although the unfortunate circumstance of the transfer of duties between ministers directed special attention to this department, in my view farmers across Canada are more interested in the discussion of these estimates because they are waiting for the government to make a definite statement of their policy for the first time with regard to this important industry.
When the minister took office last May the farmers did not expect him to be able to come forth with a new policy at once. They understood that he was new in politics and new to the administration of the Department of Agriculture, one of the larger departments of the government. But after the passing of almost 12 months the farmers feel that they are entitled to a definite statement of policy. They were not aware, of course, of the idea of transferring responsibilities. They did not know that the minister was held up in the development of a policy first of all by the fact that, as we were given to understand last May, there might be a second minister of agriculture for eastern Canada and a certain hon. member was earmarked for that very important post.
We in the opposition waited very patiently to see what would develop. No legislation was introduced to create this most important post and it was during the recess between sessions that we learned that the Minister of Forestry was going to take on the additional duties of minister of agriculture for eastern Canada. Once again the entire farm population of Canada was left in confusion because the farmers saw that once again there could be delay in the formation of a policy.

The minister has had very few opportunities in the house to put forward a definite policy on behalf of the government. Such policy as we have had has been announced in bits and pieces. It is the hope of the opposition that the minister will avail himself of this opportunity to state the policy of the government on the various aspects of agriculture for the very first time.
In the few remarks that the minister made last Thursday he spoke of ARDA, which is considered by many in Canada to be one of the most important pieces of legislation so far as the future of agriculture is concerned. The minister spoke of eight employees in his department who would be transferred, in the event of ARDA being removed from his jurisdiction. We are beginning to suspect that the government does not appreciate the magnitude of the agricultural problems that can be solved by means of the administration of this most important act. Instead of the government having only eight employees engaged in the administration of ARDA, and in investigations under that act, there could profitably be 80 employees.
One field in which this act could be of the greatest benefit to the Canadian people is that of conservation. There are many areas in Canada today where the farmers lack water, that most important and necessary of all assets in producing grain and feed for the future. Surely at a time when other countries are talking about diverting the waters of some of the largest rivers in the world in order that there may be enough water for their people the government should be able to see that right in southwestern Ontario lack of water is one of the greatest worries facing agriculture. As a matter of fact, there is talk now of a water grid for southwestern Ontario in order that the municipalities and farmers may have enough water, and under ARDA the government has a splendid vehicle to develop and promote this very necessary asset for agriculture.
I was much impressed indeed to hear the hon. member for Port Arthur state that in his opinion ARDA was being neglected. Surely that is the opinion of the entire opposition. We have the legislation, we have the vehicle, and we have a government in power that has promised to help the farmers. Here is an area where they can move effectively and with real benefit to all of Canada. Yet we have not even had a statement of policy from the government. The minister says there is no clash of personalities and that if ARDA and its eight employees are taken from his department there will be no ill feeling. Perhaps there will be no ill feeling on the part of the minister, but there is
Supp ly-A griculture
certainly a great deal of confusion and ill feeling on the part of those in this country who are experienced in agriculture.
One thing the minister dealt with was the grain policy in the east. He referred to the number of tons or bushels of grain in the east this year, thanks to the policy of the government. It is true that there is 47 per cent more grain in the east, I believe, than there was a year ago. It is true that this will probably take care of the needs of the feeders in agriculture in the east. I give the government credit for this, they showed foresight. But once again this is not a policy: It is a stopgap promotion. They were faced with a problem which they met by an emergency measure, but this does not solve anything. They gave assistance in the transportation of grain, and this is fine. They built up the storage of grain, and this is fine. But, sir, we in the opposition feel that under this program there is a possibility that many of the grain merchants will derive far more benefit than the farmers it was designed to aid.
I should like to deal with farm credit for a moment. One of the speakers who preceded me stated that there is confusion in the department with regard to this important part of the responsibilities of the Minister of Agriculture and that because of the transfer of responsibilities the department in effect did not even know to which minister it was responsible. How can responsible officials of a department carry out their duties when not only has no policy been laid down for them but they are not even sure under which department they come? It seems to me this is a most ridiculous position for agriculture to find itself in, in this day and age.
Under the present government the farmers of the country were led to believe there would be immediate changes in farm credit policy. It was stated that the amount of money available to a young farmer to keep him on the farm was not enough, that the ceiling should be raised and that legislation would be introduced to take care of this very important segment of the population. But here we are almost 12 months later, and there has not even been an announcement by the minister that such legislation is contemplated.
The price of land has gone up drastically in certain sections of Canada and we agree that the limit of $20,000 on the amount which a young farmer can borrow to buy land is not enough. We agree that something has to be done to take care of the situation and keep these young men on the land. The opposition cannot bring this about. We can only urge the government to introduce legislation, we cannot force them to do so. This is why we criticize the lack of policy today. Put the

Supply-Agriculture
legislation before us. We say to the government: Carry out your promises to the farmers, and with both sides of the house working together let us give the farmers of Canada the necessary legislation and assistance they need.
Reference has been made to crop stabilization. We have not had an announcement of policy in connection with stabilization since the minister took office, although we heard promises during the election campaign. I do not wish to go through all the promises that were made with regard to agriculture, but I should like to deal with a few of them.
I should like to speak about sugar beets for just a moment. During the last election campaign Liberal candidates said the previous administration had no policy with regard to sugar beets. One of the first things they were going to do was to formulate for the first time in Canada a definite sugar beet policy. It is now 12 months later and, goodness knows, we have had a crisis in connection with sugar during that time, but we have no policy announcement as yet from the Department of Agriculture. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said this problem is being considered. I am sure the new minister will take this problem under consideration. However the farmers of Canada want more than consideration; they want some action.
Then, what about soybeans? In my area, where soybeans are grown in large quantities, when hon. members opposite were on the hustings they said the support price for soybeans was far from adequate. They said the farmers were entitled to a support price of no less than $2.40 per bushel. Well, this government has got the price up to $2,17 per bushel, 1 cent more than it was under the previous administration. Is this the policy of the government? Is this all they intend to do? Is this the way they live up to their promises?
Today I asked the minister a question about butter, and he was courteous in his answer to me. He said they were looking into this question and it was being taken into consideration. This is not policy. We have heard today an announcement by the British government that they are going to increase the quota on butter coming into Great Britain this year by 2| per cent. This does not sound like very much, but when you realize the vast quantities of butter imported into Great Britain, 2| per cent really means thousands of tons of butter. If there is anything we have in surplus quantities in this country, it is butter. If there is anything this country can produce, it is butter. We would like the minister to say what the policy of this government is with regard to taking over a larger share of that market. We need this market, and we need this policy.

During the session last year we heard a lot about Bill No. C-5 introduced by the hon. member for Essex South. The purpose of the bill was to help farmers by guaranteeing their rights when they took their produce to canning plants. This bill was shelved. During the last days of that session the Prime Minister stood in his place and said the subject matter of the bill would be given consideration and when the Bankruptcy Act was amended provision would be made to take care of the farmers. The farmers need this protection, sir. As yet however we have had no announcement of policy; nothing has been done.
We are in the midst of the greatest evolution in the history of agriculture. Policies for agriculture that are introduced today are obsolete by tomorrow. It has been admitted that automation is creeping into agriculture. We hear about marketing schemes and about co-operatives. We hear about vertical integration, and these are new terms in connection with agriculture. As I have said, agriculture is going through a process of evolution.
The minister has mentioned what was done under the previous administration, and then he has said, "We have done this much more." This is not policy. This is nothing new. When the previous government introduced a policy for agriculture, that was not the end, Mr. Chairman, it was the beginning. The policy of this government seems to have been, whatever you were getting we are going to give you more. We have to have new ideas. We have to have new goals. We have to know what is wrong with agriculture and act upon that knowledge. This government has received briefs from the farmers' union, from the federation of agriculture and from the different commodity groups in agriculture. These men are learned men; they are technicians in connection with agriculture. They know what the questions are and what the answers are. But, Mr. Chairman, although these men have produced this information, they have produced the'studies and done the groundwork for the government, we have no policy announcements from the government as yet. The farmers are confused. We can understand why. The time is coming when the minister will have to stand in this house and say that this government has the following policy in connection with agriculture.
I am, myself, very disappointed that the administration of agriculture is to be divided. We are told that the Minister of Forestry will assume responsibility for some branches of agriculture, and that the Minister of Agriculture will retain some branches. There will be a committee of three taking responsibility for agriculture, a troika. The committee of three will be the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Forestry acting

under the chairmanship of the Minister of Agriculture. The government says this is a policy, to divide the responsibility for agriculture amongst three people, and agriculture will go forward as it never has before. This policy is inconsistent with the policy of the government in connection with the Department of National Defence because they are doing exactly the reverse in connection with that department. You cannot have it both ways. You cannot consolidate in one department and spread out in another department and call this consistent policy. I think the farmers of Canada have been very patient. They have waited for 12 months for a policy announcement to which they are entitled. These policies were promised to them. Hon. members opposite said that when they came into office they had the answers, and the farmers believed them. Now the farmers know for certain that hon. members opposite not only do not have the answers, they do not even know the questions.

Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) in his seat, because it is not often that he is seen in the house.
We on this side of the house would be very pleased to hear him define this government's policy with regard to agriculture.
On the orders of the day, I asked the minister whether he was in favour of sharing his responsibilities with another cabinet minister? The minister refused to answer, and we want to give him an opportunity of replying to a most important question while announcing this government's policy.
Mr. Chairman, the farmers are going bankrupt under this government, because it has no definite farm policy.
We do not know where we are going. In fact, last week, I asked several questions on agriculture but did not receive any answer.
We want to know why the Minister of Agriculture makes statements in the west and the Prime Minister, in answer to a question put to him, said that the Minister of Agriculture was ill. We would like to know whether the Minister of Agriculture was actually in Winnipeg a few days ago or whether he was confined at home or in the hospital as a result of illness.
Mr. Chairman, the production of cigarette tobacco in Canada is an important sector of the agricultural economy of our country. And the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) made unfortunate statements against smoking.
The consumption of cigarette tobacco in Canada has been decreasing alarmingly for some time, and I suggest that the Minister
Supply-Agriculture
of National Health and Welfare is largely responsible for this situation because she contributed to worsen it.
For the fiscal year ending March 31 last, taxes on tobacco yielded $171 million to the federal government. When the consumption of cigarette tobacco decreases, this not only directly affects a large part of the farmers, such as tobacco growers of Quebec and Ontario, but reduces also the revenue of the federal government.
I am asking the Minister of Agriculture what policy he intends to set forth to repair the considerable damage suffered by the cigarette tobacco growers as a result of the unfortunate statements of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
I read lately in a magazine that there is no evidence that tobacco is a cause of cancer, and I wonder why the Minister of National Health and Welfare ventured in such a field since she was entirely unqualified to do so.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, if consumption of cigarette tobacco decreases, the working class will be affected. I have here an article according to which the cigarette factories in Quebec are reducing their staff. That is the result of the statements made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
We, on this side of the house, would be pleased to learn from the minister what he intends to do in order to help farmers whose income is ever decreasing. All farm publications are giving the alarm to the government and asking it to take a definite stand. Mr. Chairman, how can the present government have a farm policy when the Minister of Agriculture is always absent from the house and when members of the opposition are unable to put questions to him and to ask him what he intends to do to help farmers?
Mr. Chairman, once again I am calling on the minister to answer this question: What does he intend to do to encourage agronomists and agricultural technicians from the province of Quebec to come to Ottawa to take their place in the federal Department of Agriculture?
I am also asking the Minister of Agriculture to give special attention to federal experimental stations in Canada to increase research, but not to forget experimental farms in the province of Quebec. In the last ten months, agronomists and agricultural technicians in Quebec have been leaving the experimental farms belonging to the federal government to work for the provincial government and in industry. There is, in the riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, an experimental farm which has been going downhill for some time, that is since the government came to power. I ask the minister to take the necessary steps in order to rectify

Supply-Agriculture
this situation and urge the agronomists and farm technicians to take their place in the experimental farms.
I also ask the Minister of Agriculture to increase the estimates for research in our experimental farms, and particularly in the province of Quebec.
In closing, I shall repeat in English the question I asked the minister on the orders of the day, so as to give him the opportunity to answer me:

I ask the minister if he agrees to share the responsibilities of his department with another minister? I ask him a direct question and give him an opportunity to answer right now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue.

Mr. Chairman, in order to allow the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) to consider what answer he should give the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), I shall take a few minutes to put a few questions concerning the agricultural policy of the government.
To begin with, could the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) explain satisfactorily his complete silence during his budget speech with regard to farmers' needs. I consider this failure on the part of the Minister of Finance a real disgrace. I should like to know why, to a question asking him for an explanation, the minister merely said in his usual offhand manner: "Well, farmers have children-" That was a reference to the fact that from now on, family allowances would be extended to students of 16 and 17 years of age.
But the Minister of Finance has refused to understand the needs of a basic industry in our country. Neither he nor the Minister of Agriculture have been able to give us satisfactory answers on that matter.
Mr. Chairman, I was dismayed, on Thursday, to hear the Minister of Agriculture take

the credit for the enactment of the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. We have noted this completely unfounded assertion on the part of the minister. If he wants to take the responsibility and the credit for this legislation, he should give it the necessary understanding to make it efficient. I say, it has been one of the finest gestures on the part of the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. Hamilton), to plan this legislation and later have it passed and, in doing so, to have prepared the ground for a renewal of the rural and agricultural development in this country. But it was not enough to have a grandiose plan and to understand the actual needs of the farmers; it was necessary, once that legislation was passed, to implement it, to reach the necessary agreements with the various provinces and to really make it one of the mainstays of the whole agricultural policy.
Well, the Minister of Agriculture, by his ill-founded assertions on that subject, saying that only eight people looked after the implementation of that act, proved that he did not have the slightest idea of the possibilities of the said act, that he could not care less and, what is even more serious, that he did not understand the needs of the farmers and the rural population.
Mr. Chairman, a few moments ago, I heard the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), with whom I seldom agree. I agree with him when he says that the farmers' needs are tremendous. He has singled out my own riding which is essentially a rural one. He expressed high hopes concerning the application of the ARDA program because, in his opinion, this legislation is one of the ways by which the now extremely urgent transformation of the agricultural and rural areas will come through.
Mr. Chairman, this does not only concern farm land as such, it has to do with a greater problem, namely the adaptation of the rural areas, including not only tillable and farm land, but also villages and the vast spaces surrounding the farm areas of our country, particularly in the province of Quebec.
With ARDA, we see the possibility, first of all, of transforming into profitable units farms which are no longer an economic proposition; second, the possibility of creating new rural industries; third, the possibility of employing advantageously farm labour and farmers' children.
The needs of the agricultural class in Canada's rural districts are immeasurable. The farmer is at the crossroads. He has to face an increasing cost of living, scarce manpower,

difficulties in supplying himself, at reasonable prices, with feed grains and in securing the machinery required for his farm.
All these problems are essential parts of the rural and agricultural problem. This government does not seeem to understand these basic problems, and that is the reason why the rural districts are still depressed.
Whether it is the present Minister of Agriculture who carries out the responsibility of rural rehabilitation, or whether it is handled by the Minister of Forestry-who is now sitting in his seat-it matters very little. Personally, I think that may be the Minister of Forestry is more capable of handling this problem and also to understand it by putting it in its proper perspective. But whoever is handling it, the government must face up to its responsibilities and must avoid deceiving the sanguine hopes that have been given the agricultural and the rural people by the former parliament when they passed the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act called ARDA.
That is why I join with all those who spoke before me and I urge the government to act resolutely and intelligently in carrying out this program and helping the many farmers scattered throughout the country, many of them in the province of Quebec and in my own riding, who were extremely disappointed by carelessness of the present government toward the agricultural class.
I feel that the government is confirming its indifference towards these problems by allowing the Minister of Finance to present a budget which ignores completely the rightful needs of the agricultural class.

services are? Is this a salary or a payroll item and, if so, does it represent payments made to people in the public service, or are these payments to consultants or outsiders? I am glad the minister has started to answer some questions. The questions he answered were comparatively trivial. He has been asked for a statement on agricultural policy-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: On a point of order, I do not think that questions asked about items in the estimates, while the committee is scrutinizing the estimates, should be called trivial. That is what we are here for.

I am glad the hon. gentleman has come back to the view that these are matters of importance, and that is the reason for the stand we took the other day- not over a matter of $30,000 or $40,000 or $70,000 but over a matter of $140 million which the government endeavoured to have passed without opportunity for proper debate.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: It is $240 million.

Yes, $240 million and I am glad the hon. gentleman joins with us now because, after all, these things are important.
I ask in what circumstances we were brought back here. Why should we have been brought back here? Because we decide to

Supply-Agriculture
take a stand and demand that full opportunity be given to parliament to examine this expenditure of $240 million? We were told, after gross delay on the part of the Minister of Finance: We shall sit tonight for a couple of hours and if you do not pass these estimates then in effect you will have to deny yourselves the holiday which is customarily allowed at Easter time. Indeed the carrot is still before us in the motion which rests on the order paper, reading:
That immediately after royal assent has been given to the hill providing for the appropriation based on supplementary estimates (E), this house adjourn until Monday, April 6, 1964.
The only reason for that motion being there is to dangle it in front of us as a carrot to bring about the passage of this vast amount of money.
Is it a carrot, or a club?

I will come to that. It is dangled in front of us as a carrot to bring about the passage of this vast amount of money without the fullest examination, and we have had no information on these matters. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings said, "Is it a club?" They tried the club the other day, and it did not work. Now they have added the carrot to the club in the motion in question.
I intend to refer to the fact that here we are asked to pass these items, the indication being that we are to pass them before March 31. It is of interest to see sitting opposite the genial Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Transport. I like to look back and take the views that they expressed only two years ago-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Just before an election.
-for after all, by their past you can judge them. They claim, by inference, that these supplementary accounts have to be passed by March 31. Nothing of the kind.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I ask the
right hon. gentleman whether he would assist my memory. Was not that just before the election?

Oh, Mr. Chairman. See, the rules are different when the opposition indulges in this kind of action just before an election. We do not believe in that; we believe that the rules are the same before or after an election.
I want to be helpful. I just wanted to get some information.
I beg your pardon?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was just asking for some historical information. Was it just before the election?

I will come to that in a moment. That indicates the philosophy the hon. gentleman has always had; that if it is before an election, whether it is right or wrong, wrong as it is it is always right if it suits his purpose. He has apparently forgotten the situation. But I am here to say why, under this general item, parliament is not going to allow itself to be browbeaten by those people sitting opposite. Let that be clear. Let me point out also that there was no reason for the recalling of the house today by the pleaded necessity that these estimates have to be passed by March 31.
I shall refer to what happened in 1962. We brought in the final supplementaries in the middle of March. We started to debate them. Some $138 million was involved. We said they could be passed in a matter of three days, and they were debated on March 28, 29 and 30. The Liberal party that today is in office was then in opposition, and I may identify personally these distinguished representatives, if they feel it desirable that they should receive that attention. I point out that we did not take the stand they had to be passed. We said it was a fine objective that they should pass; the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said, "That is our objective", but in no way pressed the necessity of passage. They were not concluded in any way. The debate went ahead for three days. The then opposition, the government of today, debated these estimates at length. They did not have the views that the Minister of Justice has today, that parliament has to pass these items before the end of the fiscal year. That was not their view then. The debate continued on April 6, 12, 13 and 16. I think this has to be very definitely underlined and emphasized. As a matter of fact, the appropriation bill was not passed until after consideration on April 17 and 18. I mention this because there are some people endeavouring to leave the impression that because the end of the fiscal year is approaching, we have to pass these items; that they have to be passed before March 31. Nothing of the kind. I want to make that clear.
The only reason we were brought back here is that the government, and particularly the Minister of Justice, found themselves in an impossible position in moving that the house should sit on Good Friday and then again had to beat one of those retreats to which the government has become so addicted. It is a very interesting position. On Thursday, he did not know where to go, and said, "We will come back tomorrow". Then within an hour the Prime Minister, realizing the

nature of the step that was being taken, announced, "Of course we will not sit on Good Friday". Now we are back here, and we intend to examine these items fully and completely; let that be clear. We do not intend to accept the carrot now being held out with regard to the Easter recess. We intend to examine these items, and if we do not get any more information than we have got so far, it is going to take quite a while.
I can realize the position of the Minister of Finance. He has tried very hard; he has no doubt endeavoured to bring about reductions, and yet the harder he tries, the greater the increase in the expenditures. I can well understand the position of the Prime Minister. When speaking in Toronto on March 14 to a gathering of his party he said, "Poor Walter Gordon is going to bring his budget in on Monday. Surely we can spare him just a moment of silent prayer".
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I just want to thank all hon. members.

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE EMERGENCY AMBULANCE SERVICES
SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE EMERGENCY AMBULANCE SERVICES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of amending the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to provide for payment, in agreement with the provinces, for emergency ambulance services.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this private members' notice of motion I should like to review ambulance services as they now exist across Canada. In the city of St. John's, Newfoundland, ambulance services are operated by the government with the aid of a federal grant. In the province of Nova Scotia ambulance services are generally provided by the funeral directors in the province. This is also true in the province of Prince Edward Island. In the province of New Brunswick the major hospitals in the larger cities run ambulance services, but in the smaller towns these services are again run by the funeral directors. In the province of Quebec most of the ambulance services are provided by the funeral directors, and in the city of Montreal they are covered by police ambulances.
In the province of Ontario the provision of ambulance service is quite varied. In the city of Toronto the city itself owns and operates a municipally controlled ambulance service. In Oakville, the town in which I live, the ambulance service is subsidized by the town at a cost to the town of $12,000 a year. In addition of course the ambulance operator charges the normal ambulance fees, but the operation is still a losing proposition. In the town of Georgetown, also in my riding, the ambulance and ambulance quarters are provided by the municipality itself and the 20220-99
Suggested Provision for Ambulance Services ambulance service staff is made up of volunteers from the town. They are unpaid and provide a 24 hour, efficient, trained ambulance service.
In the province of Manitoba, Winnipeg has a combination of public and private ambulances. In the rest of the province ambulance service is provided, generally speaking, by funeral directors. In Saskatchewan there is some provincial legislation requiring that drivers of ambulances must be trained in first aid. In the cities of Saskatchewan the ambulance services are subsidized while in the rest of the province services are again provided by funeral directors. In the province of Alberta there is provincial legislation covering drivers and equipment but not the ambulance vehicles themselves. In that part of the province outside of the cities service is provided by funeral directors. In the province of British Columbia the situation is well taken care of in the city of Vancouver, but in the rest of the province there is a varied amount of coverage. In some areas coverage is provided by the municipalities and in other areas by the fire departments.
In reviewing the provincial situation I would point out that eight out of the ten provinces have no legislation on their statute books covering ambulance services, vehicles or the training necessary for the people who operate ambulances. The basic problem is a financial one and it is to cover the financial problem that I have proposed this notice of motion today. If the financial problems were solved, ambulance operators could provide good vehicles, adequate equipment and adequately trained personnel.
As I have mentioned, there are basically three types of ambulance service provided in Canada. The first is that provided by funeral directors as an extension of their funeral services, but funeral directors are gradually leaving the ambulance business because it is not profitable. For years dead people have actually been subsidizing injured people. The funeral directors have been providing ambulance service out of their other income and they are gradually drifting out of the business. The second group comprises those who provide privately operated ambulance services. These operations are so unprofitable that in many areas the operators have been subsidized by the municipalities. The third group is composed of the publicly operated ambulance services which are directly operated and controlled by municipalities.
As I have mentioned, the private enterprise ambulance operators cannot make a living, or if they do they find it impossible to provide proper vehicles and the proper training for their drivers in order to make the service
1564	HOUSE OF
Suggested Provision for Ambulance Services adequate. What is needed first of all is legislation regarding minimum standards of vehicles, equipment and trained personnel. This is a provincial responsibility and I am not going to discuss it further. However, I should like to say in passing that in Ontario a committee has been set up by the provincial government after representations from the ambulance operators, the medical association of Ontario and the chamber of commerce.
The second thing that is needed, and which I would hope to cover by this motion, is financing. I am convinced that if we can solve the financial problem the other problems will straighten themselves out. The resolution reads in part as follows:
-to provide for payment, in agreement with the provinces, for emergency ambulance services.
The resolution would bring emergency ambulance services under the terms of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. The words "for emergency ambulance services" are included to prevent ambulances being used as a glorified taxi service. This wording is used to ensure that those who suffer an accident or sudden illness will be transported quickly to where they can obtain medical aid and so that ambulance fees will not be covered in the case of people who may have to go to a hospital for a blood test or who are being admitted for something that is not of an urgent nature.
As I mentioned, generally speaking ambulance services in the past have been provided by funeral directors who are gradually getting out of the business. People who are involved in accidents are often not very eager to pay for ambulance service and their reason for not wanting to pay is a justifiable one. When people are injured in an automobile accident they do not call the ambulance and therefore they do not feel that they should be required to pay for the ambulance service. Statistics show that in some areas as high as 90 per cent of ambulance service fees, which would normally be collected as the result of the use of ambulances after accidents, are actually never collected.
While one does not like to speak of money with regard to such an important, humanitarian operation as the provision of ambulance services for the people of Canada, without fees dedicated ambulance drivers and operators cannot stay in the business. My answer to the problem, which is not the only solution but is one that would serve the purpose very well, is to include bona fide emergency ambulance services under the terms of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. This measure would also provide for better ambulance service in that proper vehicles would be used. I am not sure how many members are aware of the


situation but in some remote rural areas ambulance services are actually provided by jeeps or trucks or station wagons with a blanket and stretcher in them.
Some ambulance operators carry no emergency equipment at all. I believe most medical people feel that all ambulances should carry emergency equipment such as oxygen, first aid equipment and what is called suction equipment. It is also generally agreed that the people who operate ambulances should be trained in rudimentary first aid. Not very long ago in a riding close to mine a person was brought to a hospital who almost died on the trip there as a result of her injury. The fact is that her injury only amounted to a cut on her head from which she almost bled to death. The bleeding could have been stopped very easily and simply by the application of the most rudimentary first aid.
It is often said, Mr. Speaker, that "accident" is only a word until you have one. When and if you do have one, Mr. Speaker, this motion would see to it that you would be well looked after and it would help to provide the best of care for the people of Canada.
