speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE EMERGENCY AMBULANCE SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make some remarks on the motion proposed by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley). The motion before the house is one relating to emergency ambulance services, and I think it should be distinguished from ambulance services merely for the transportation of a non-emergency patient from his home to the hospital or from one hospital to another. I think the definition of the word "emergency" given by the hon. member for Halton is rather imprecise. We have to be more precise in defining these words "emergency ambulance services".
After reading some material available on this subject, Mr. Speaker, the general view is that provincial legislation is required to set minimum standards for the training of the attendants of these ambulances and for the type of equipment necessary to handle traffic casualty cases and medical emergencies. There also has to be control, especially, of communications because many problems have arisen as a result of lack of communication between police centres and ambulance centres and the emergency departments of our hospitals. Many times we have seen ambulances bring traffic casualty cases or sick persons to a hospital and the hospital has had to deny the patient admission because of

lack of space or lack of the necessary equipment to deal with the particular case. We have found the ambulance had already left and we had to phone for another ambulance to take this patient to another hospital.
In Alberta legislation covering ambulance services has been provided through the department of highways. In Saskatchewan legislation covering ambulance services is provided under the public health act. In several municipalities civic legislation has been passed to deal with this problem. Some critics say that a firm, clear provincial policy regarding the financing of ambulance service is long overdue, and that this is really the main problem. The previous speaker stated that today many ambulance services are provided by funeral directors and so they are provided at the expense of the dead.
I am sure however that the members of this house are in agreement there should be a very profound study conducted of this whole field of ambulance services. These services provide not only transportation for the patient but also, in many cases, treatment. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley) stated I believe that many people could die of haemorrhage or other medical complications while being transported from the scene of an accident or from a home to a hospital.
In discussing the financial implications of providing emergency ambulance service, we should review the principles of hospital insurance based on the traditional patterns in force at that time and which are still in force, when the present hospital insurance program was first being planned. Subsequent discussion with interested bodies involved in the provision of hospital services revealed that it was accepted as a basic principle of the Canadian scheme that the new legislation entitled the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act would have regard to the traditional patterns of providing hospital services, and the traditional patterns in relation to each of those services across this country. Thus the present plan, while financed from premiums of the public which have been supplemented by the federal-provincial governments, has respected the autonomy of the hospital.
This perhaps is not unrelated to the question of ambulance services. However, the traditional Canadian pattern of providing these services has been based primarily on private or public ownership, but not by hospitals. In a survey carried out in Ontario a few years ago, it was ascertained that 90 per cent of the ambulance services provided in that province were privately owned, and to some extent were carried out as sidelines 20220-99J
Suggested Provision for Ambulance Services to a principal business. The number of ambulance services owned and operated by hospitals in Canada is minimal.
Our federal-provincial hospital insurance program was designed to cover those services which by custom and by tradition comprised services normally associated with hospitals. Those do not include ambulance services. The pattern of separating ambulance services from hospital services is not an exclusive feature of the federal hospital plan. This nonambulance feature was also followed by its predecessor in the provincial hospital programs of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. The separation of the two services is due to the fact that while part of the duties of ambulance service have some relationship to hospital services, those are only a very small part of the over-all services. It has been regarded that ambulance services are closely related to other public services in a community, for example firefighting services and their ambulances, and police services, especially regarding highway traffic cases.
It has been suggested that ambulance services should be the subject of special legislation at the municipal or provincial level, containing provisions covering the licensing of the ambulance firm, the staff of the ambulance, the equipping of the ambulance, and communication facilities. None of these provisions would be in any way related to hospitals, but these services should operate under the direction or the supervision of the medical association. Under hospital insurance, costs which are included as shareable operating costs are those which form the normal part of the operating budgets of hospitals. Since ambulance services were usually not within the normal budgets of hospitals, those costs were excluded from those considered shareable.
In addition to the problem of costs, there are other problems associated with ambulance services and these mitigate against their inclusion in a hospital insurance program. These problems relate to the necessary controls which are essential in administering a program supported by public funds. I would suggest that these controls relate both to the utilization and also the quality of the ambulance service. With regard to the utilization of ambulance service, if associated with hospital insurance it would be necessary to define what distances and in what circumstances and under whose endorsement public funds could be used. In the absence of precise and enforceable regulations, the costs of hospital insurance for services not necessarily related to hospital care, which is the criterion for the receipt of insured services, would

Suggested Provision for Ambulance Services impose on hospital costs an element very difficult, it not impossible for the hospitals to control.
Second, the control of quality or the basic standards for ambulances is also a problem which has been recognized but which I think comes within the purview, of municipal and provincial governments. In Ontario, the provincial attorney general has recognized this need of raising standards and has recently given consideration to the demands of the Ontario ambulance operators association and the Ontario medical association. He stated that a profound study should be carried out to improve ambulance services in Ontario, and that this study is entirely separate from anything related to hospital insurance.
There is no doubt that ambulance services are urgently in need of improvement, including a satisfactory solution of the problem of paying for the ambulance services rendered, but this need should not be confused with the availability of funds for the program of hospital insurance. The royal commission on health services has been studying Canada's health service needs on a broad basis, and I expect its report will deal with the question of ambulance services. Meanwhile this problem should be reviewed on the local level as an essential need in the public service area.
There have been a few regional and two national studies of the ambulance services conducted in Canada. In 1955 there was the Montreal conference which studied the medical aspects of traffic accidents. In 1960 there was the Cornwall area traffic casualty study. In 1963 there was the brief of the Ontario ambulance operators association, and also in that year the communication services study in initial care and transportation in medical emergencies, conducted by the National Academy of Sciences. However, these studies have been rather limited in scope and did not result in significant action.
It is essential that more information be published on ambulance services, and these should be investigated in detail by the medical profession of Canada prior to recommending the courses open to governmental authorities in providing both improved and financially feasible ambulance services for Canadians. Among the things that should be studied are the ambulance services provided by the federal government.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, there are many federal departments which provide ambulance services. They include the Department of National Defence, the Department of Veterans Affairs which transports its patients from their homes to the veterans hospitals, the Department of National Health and Welfare which provides ambulance services in

remote areas, and the Department of Transport. As I stated previously, municipal governments in many cases provide ambulance services through their fire, police and public health departments.
Very few of the hospitals in Canada provide ambulance services. These ambulance services for emergency cases are very popular in many city hospitals in large United States metropolitan centres like New York city and Los Angeles. Such ambulances are provided by the emergency department of a hospital and are staffed by junior interns on duty in the hospital's emergency department.
With regard to the financial arrangements of paying for ambulance services, I must say that the fees are rather high. In the city of Toronto where I practised medicine for several years, the fee was $15 for a one-way trip from the home to the hospital or from the hospital to another hospital, no matter what the distance was within the city limits. At present in Toronto there are nine municipal public health ambulances and 29 ambulances provided by private concerns. Although the availability of ambulances is satisfactory, following the study and recommendations made by the Toronto city council's department of health, it has been shown that there is however a crying need for provincial legislation to provide better equipment for ambulances.
It is said that these days $12,000 is required for a properly equipped ambulance. As stated by the hon. member for Halton, only 8 per cent of the ambulances in Ontario are equipped with oxygen service. So far as I am concerned every ambulance should be equipped with oxygen service and personnel who know how to use oxygen equipment. It may be necessary for people who are severely breathless or who are in shock from acute coronary thrombosis.
Although as I have said, the ambulance services in Toronto are adequate, they are too expensive. A fee of $15 is a lot of money for a person to pay to be transported from his home to a hospital. I sympathize with the view expressed by the hon. member for Halton that some provision should be made to make it financially easy on patients to get ambulance services. However, in view of the fact that his motion states that this should be paid for through the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act I must say, apart from the point which I stressed before, that it was not the traditional pattern for hospitals to provide ambulance services. This whole area of hospital insurance will, we hear, be studied at the forthcoming federal-provincial conference in Quebec city.
Apparently many provinces wish to opt out of the shared programs, and the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act is one

of these shared programs. Therefore it is expected that this problem of emergency ambulance services will come solely under the jurisdiction of the provinces, and they will have to deal both with legislation controlling the quality of ambulances as well as paying for the costs.

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE EMERGENCY AMBULANCE SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that this notice of motion, to the effect that the government should consider the advisability of amending the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, in order to provide, with the provinces, for the payment of emergency ambulance services, represents a new invasion in fields reserved exclusively to the provinces.
Such a legislative measure would impose new taxes on us, at both levels, federal and provincial.
It would create a double bureaucracy, an administration in Ottawa and an administration in Quebec or in any other province.
If the government, through this joint program, wants to give financial help to the provinces for the setting up of such a system, which is the responsibility of the municipalities and provinces concerned, and not of the federal government, it need not invent a new plan, or devise a new tax; all it has to do is to give financial help to the provinces to enable them to manage themselves as far as hospital insurance and all such details including emergency ambulance service, are concerned.
I do not believe at all that such a notice of motion is likely to facilitate the decentralization which everybody agrees should be implemented more and more in this country. Instead, we should introduce notices of motion which would definitely help the provinces.
Then, we could talk of respect for provincial autonomy, of federal decentralization, which becomes more and more urgent. We see in all these notices of motion a new invasion in fields coming under provincial jurisdiction.
As far as we are concerned, we object to the adoption of such a motion because we think it would be a duplication of jurisdiction which would impose new taxes.
Clearly, the Canadian people cannot pay any more than it does at the present time.
If, as I said a while ago, the federal government wants to be useful, I suggest it should supply the funds required by the provinces, while giving them full discretion to administer themselves with their own structures.
The federal government does not know where to get the necessary funds or credits to assist the provinces in the administration
Suggested Provision for Ambulance Services of such a deal. There is only one way out, the government must turn to the Bank of Canada, where it will find the credits required for the expansion and the administration of the provinces, municipalities and well organized public bodies, including the federal government.
Then, there would be no intrusion by the federal government into fields reserved to provinces, or in the administration of municipalities. Rather, there would be understanding, and I think the federal government would be giving assistance to the provinces. That way, the federal government would be carrying out the function for which it exists.
The federal government does not exist to penalize the provinces or take decisions for them, but to encourage their development in their own and respective fields.
The passing of such a motion, as such a piece of legislation would be neither more nor less than an additional infringement on that freedom which definitely belongs to the provinces.
I shall not labour that point any longer, because some other hon. members have indicated their desire to make themselves heard. I see that even Liberals are anxious to reach six o'clock so that the motion will not be passed. I leave it to them to talk out that motion.

subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE EMERGENCY AMBULANCE SERVICES
speechtext:
Two of
the three previous speakers are members of the medical profession and you, Mr. Speaker, may have noticed the divergency of opinion which exists even in the medical profession on the question raised by this notice of motion.
I am not a member of the medical profession but I claim some knowledge of the ambulance situation as it exists in Canada today, and I wish to rise in protest against the implications of the motion before us. I note that the previous speaker, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) commented on the fact that even members of the Liberal party appear anxious to have this particular motion talked out. I would not use that phrase myself, but I would advise the hon. member for Villeneuve that I am against the motion for reasons which I shall advance and which I hold to be good ones.
I do not like to talk about myself. On the other hand, one does get first hand knowledge from personal experience, and I must say that there is one word in this motion which causes me a great deal of difficulty, and that is the word "emergency". The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of amending the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic
1568	HOUSE OF
Suggested Provision for Ambulance Services Services Act to provide for payment, in agreement with the provinces, for emergency ambulance services.
I have to ask: What is an emergency? I happen in private life to be connected with a hospital which maintains more than 240 beds, that is to say it is a fair sized institution. I only wish that we received 100 per cent cooperation from each and every member of the medical staff of that institution. There are more than 100 doctors on the staff and it is interesting to see what a few of them will resort to in order to put patients of their own into hospital. I know that the experiences I shall recite are not isolated cases but that they can be duplicated throughout Canada from coast to coast, day after day. We operate an emergency department-a division which not all hospitals possess-and doctors will call up with a paying patient who is really anxious to get to hospital. After all, the patient is paying his premiums under the Ontario hospital services act and feels he is entitled to a bed when he requires it. But there is no bed available in the hospital with which the doctor is connected. However, the doctor knows that emergency cases are admitted to hospital for immediate treatment, and if there is no bed available an emergency case will be taken in and put on a wheeled apparatus known as an emergency bed; it is not a full width bed but people connected with hospitals know what I mean when I talk about these emergency beds in which emergency cases are placed.
So a doctor calls up to see if he can get a patient admitted to hospital and he is advised that there are no beds available; the patient will have to wait for two days, or two weeks, or a month, perhaps. The patient is still screaming that he requires attention. The doctor tells the patient: If you have a relative who will call an ambulance and get you taken to the hospital in an ambulance and ask that you be treated in the emergency division, you are in. So, if a doctor has an elective case on his hands, medical or surgical, all he has to do is to advise the relatives to engage an ambulance and send it to the emergency division of the hospital he designates, and the patient is admitted. Is that an emergency case or not? It may be that there has been premeditation, possibly for hours, maybe for a day or two.
What is an emergency? I witnessed one case in the last 12 weeks which may interest hon. members. A man collapsed in a church I was attending. He was at the back of the building and the thud with which he fell attracted the attention of a doctor in the congregation. The doctor immediately went to the man's assistance. The patient was lying prone on the floor, and was carried upon a stretcher into the vestry. He was in poor condition and


the doctor himself telephoned for an ambulance to take him to hospital. The ambulance arrived in about 15 minutes and took this chap to the hospital where he was placed in the emergency ward, because there were no other beds available. I personally visited this man who had collapsed in church. I asked the doctors who were attending him about his condition and they told me the patient was in a highly nervous state; the man was in a state of shock rather than anything else. Nevertheless the doctor who had attended the man in the church had called for an ambulance when this man was lying prone on the floor. The doctors at the hospital said it was a case of high nervous tension. Was that an emergency case? I asked the ambulance operator whether or not he was being paid for this service and he advised me that when he spoke to the man in this case he was told he had no money, and since he had not called for the ambulance he did not intend to pay. This was quite all right with the hospital. When I spoke to the doctor who had called for the ambulance, he pointed out that many ambulance calls are never paid for and he regretted that he had been the one who had called the ambulance. The house might be interested to know that the only cheque I ever received from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation

and that was for $25, less income tax of $1.25-reached me a week after this ambulance case, and I paid for the ambulance call myself because the ambulance operator stated he would not be paid for it; he could tell from the shape of things as they were.
There are two questions that arise here. Was the man an emergency case? I say he was not. The doctor who called him in the first instance thought he was. The doctors who treated the patient at the hospital said he was not, and no one was going to pay for the service until a volunteer came along. You cannot make a proper distinction of what is an emergency service compared with one that is non-emergency or elective.
I have the honour and pleasure to represent the riding of York-Humber, and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Gelber) and I share a municipality with a population of 130,000. The township of York is about equally divided between York South and York-Humber. Some years ago when a hospital was first constructed in the township of York, the York Lions club, who met at the Oakwood hotel, conceived the very, very charitable idea of providing an ambulance for the conveyance of injured and sick persons to the hospital. They took the idea of providing an ambulance from the East York Lions club, which is in the riding of the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto), and they raised the money, about $7,000, and gave a

brand new ambulance to the police department of York township. This was before the metropolitan Toronto amalgamation came into effect. The police department of York township-which co-operates in every way with the Northwestern hospital-agreed to operate this small ambulance as a police cruiser. It had an extension inside, on which an injured person could be laid as on a bed; the rear opened up, as ambulance doors do, and many cases were transported to hospital in this combined police cruiser and ambulance donated by the York Lions club. But when metropolitan Toronto amalgamation came into effect the police departments were amalgamated early and the new police commissioners for metropolitan Toronto stated that ambulance service was not one of the functions of a police department. They said, "We cannot have these policemen running around and going off to hospital with sick and injured people. There might be a bank robbery and, heaven knows it is better to protect money than take an injured man to hospital, so they will have to stop operating an ambulance service in the police department".
Faced with the position of having a fully paid for ambulance that the police commissioners said could not be operated by the police department, the good people of York township decided to approach the fire department. We now have in the township of York a small ambulance which looks somewhat like a district fire chief's car, but it is a combination ambulance and district fire chief's car and it gives very, very fine service to the people of York who are transferred to the hospital. The point I would like to emphasize in this connection is that of manpower. In trying to keep this ambulance, which had been donated in the first place by the York Lions club, available 24 hours a day it was necessary to contact men who would be able to answer emergency calls at any hour of the day or night. That is why the police were first contacted, and then we went to the fire department. It is now operated by the fire department of York. The mover of this motion wants the act amended so that ambulance services will be paid for by the province and the dominion; but one of the great costs here is that of providing service 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
I am quite surprised that the member for Halton has brought this motion forward at this time, just when the dominion-provincial conference is going to be renewed at Quebec city. We are told that there are two items of great interest on the agenda. The first has to do with the Canada pension plan and the second has to do with shared costs of services rendered by the federal government
Suggested Provision for Ambulance Services and the provinces. To carry a motion such as this at this time would simply be adding extra expense to these shared costs, and anyone who is in touch with current thinking in this country of ours knows that there are at least ten provinces out of ten seeking to get more control of the shared costs which they now enjoy with federal participation.
I do not think the federal government should approach the provinces at all with regard to increasing the expense under the hospital insurance acts of the provinces or under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Insurance Act. Many of the hospitals in the Dominion of Canada do not conduct emergency departments of their own, and if there is an accident on the street, to what hospital are you going to send the case even if you have an ambulance at your beck and call? It is quite possible to send an emergency case to a hospital that refuses to take it in. I know hospitals in the city of Toronto that will not accept an emergency case because they are not staffed to handle emergencies 24 hours a day. If ambulance service were paid for under the insurance plans of the provinces and the Dominion of Canada, we would be receiving calls for emergency ambulance service at all hours of the day and night, with the patient directing the ambulance as to what hospital he was to be taken, whether or not that hospital had emergency service.
The problems that arise in connection with conducting an ambulance service are insoluble when you consider that not every doctor is allowed to practise in every hospital. If a doctor has privileges in one hospital, it is seldom that he has privileges in another. A man who considered himself an emergency case, called for an ambulance and demanded to be taken to a certain hospital, might be designating a hospital in which his own doctor did not have privileges, and he would be separated from the service of his doctor, whom he has possibly been visiting for 20 or 30 years.
I cannot see how the people of Canada can be expected to pay for emergency ambulance service without everyone demanding an ambulance ride to the hospital. Then how long would it be before they would be demanding an ambulance ride home from the hospital? I have enough contacts with the relatives of patients to be able to tell the house that if there was available free ambulance service under any insurance scheme, the relatives of patients would point out that we should send their father, their husband, their wife, their daughter, their nephew or their niece home in an ambulance because the taxi ride would be far too rough; and if they were taken home in their own, broken down car they would not know whether the car would make it

Suggested Provision for Ambulance Services home. These people would say that the mother should be sent home in the ambulance. Therefore this service would not only be to the hospital but would also be from the hospital.
One of the main reasons for the shortage of hospital beds throughout the Dominion of Canada today is the fact that we have prepaid hospital insurance. People who never went to hospital before, in the voluntary pay days, are now covered by hospital insurance through the province or the dominion and are demanding hospital service when they have the slightest cold, the slightest itch or the slightest ache. Not only do they find doctors who will put them into hospitals, but they stay there for days and days unnecessarily. We have found that people who have prepaid hospital coverage squeeze it to the last possible drop, which creates a bed shortage in hospitals throughout the Dominion of Canada.
I can assure hon. members that if we had free ambulance service to hospitals, because every patient would be demanding ambulance service to hospital we would not have enough room on the highways for the ambulances that would be required to transport these patients to hospital and, in short order, to transport them home again.
I think this resolution would be incapable of fulfilment if it were passed. I agree with the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) and also the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz), who pointed out that this was an intrusion on provincial rights. I think the federal government should stay well out of this scheme as it has been advanced to us. We are told that funeral directors who operate ambulance services are going bankrupt, as well as people who operate private ambulance services. There are times when I think that that is the only reason that could be advanced for asking the federal government to step into the field; and I make the statement that if people will not pay for ambulance service when it is conducted by funeral directors or by ambulance service people when it is conducted by private entrepreneurs, there is no reason under the sun why they will be willing to pay for ambulance service through taxation under a federal-provincial scheme.
We have heard doctors point out that every ambulance should be equipped with oxygen and suction pumps. As a hospital trustee I have been quite interested in the number of times a hospital is criticized because it does not supply an intern to ride with every hospital ambulance which goes out on a call. Some people maintain that no ambulance should answer a call unless it carries a doctor to look after the patient on the way to the hospital. Pretty soon ambulances will be


running on as costly a basis hour by hour as the hospitals, and heaven knows the cost of that is breaking the back of the average Canadian taxpayer.
I am entirely opposed to this notice of motion and I sincerely ask the house to give it short shrift.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard many reasons advanced in support of the motion, although my colleague the hon. member for York-Hum-ber (Mr. Cowan) is apparently opposed to it. I feel that the hon. member who introduced the motion has done a great service in calling attention to a serious national problem. In addition to its being a national problem it is also a problem which has to be developed very carefully in light of our present day constitutional arrangements. However, I feel that the argument of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), who suggested that this was a provincial responsibility and that the federal government should stay out of it, but that the federal government should go to the Bank of Canada and get enough money to pay for an ambulance service, is as unique as anything I have heard for some time.
Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I think this is a good motion. I think the intent of the mover of the motion to bring attention to the problem is an entirely worthy one. But as the hon. member for York-Humber pointed out, there will shortly be, in a matter of days, an important federal-provincial conference, and one of the items on the agenda of that conference is the future of the shared-cost programs. The principle of shared-cost programs is inherent in the motion itself, because it calls upon this house to-
-give consideration to the advisability of amending the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to provide for payment, in agreement with the provinces, for emergency ambulance services.
Not very long ago in this house during private members' hour I personally opposed the extension of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to the field of tuberculosis hospitalization. The reason I opposed it is exactly the reason why I think this motion is a good one. It is because the whole role of federally granted aid funds should be in terms of encouragement of the development of services, to cover the gaps which currently exist and to encourage the development of standards in a co-operative arrangement, which means the signing of an agreement between the federal and provincial authorities which pays regard to variations from one province to another, from one circumstance to another, and from one coast to another in this great and diversified country which is Canada.

The principle of grants in aid was a device by which better standards were developed, by which we overcame deficiencies in our welfare and health services. When we talk about grants in aid of tuberculosis today we would not require another dollar for care. It would simply be a measure of fiscal relief to the provincial authorities, because there are now adequate beds to take care of those afflicted with this illness. Standards have been developed to attack this problem which have shown encouraging results.
I feel it is wrong for the federal authorities to move purely in the direction of fiscal relief. Fiscal relief is a matter for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to discuss within the framework of federal grants to the provinces. But when we talk of development and extension of services-in this instance I think this principle is fundamental-it is surely an area for the use of the grant in aid device.
We have heard various hon. members describe the great gaps existing in the provision of ambulance service today. In some instances they are provided by funeral directors. I submit that the skill required for the normal exercise of the function of a funeral director is rather different in nature and quality from the skill one would expect from the operator of an emergency ambulance service. In other instances this service is provided by private firms, in some other cases by municipal sponsorships, and in other cases on an irregular basis by fire and police departments.
I was formerly, Mr. Speaker, a member of the council of the city of Ottawa and I was surprised at the degree to which some private operators, who really believed in the work they were doing, put up with inconvenience and serious personal financial loss to provide the standard of service which they felt was very much needed in their community. I had the opportunity of reviewing at one stage the financial statement of a private operator, and I was astonished at the cases in which it was simply impossible for this private operator to collect bills which he had rendered, for reasons such as those so eloquently described by previous speakers in the house.
I think it is quite clear that we cannot expect such a service to be provided, logically and completely, by private enterprise, which would meet the standards we require. When the United Kingdom, in a logical pattern following the second world war, set about providing a health plan with broad coverage, they did not decide that ambulance services should be part of hospital services. This became a local authority service and it was given a very different type of structure and

Mr. Chairman, I was dealing with the general item and now I come

Supply-Agriculture
down to the particulars asked tor with regard to the Department of Agriculture. I am dealing now with the bifurcation that took place in respect of which we have so far had little or no information. I should like to know what arrangements have been made in connection with this division of power. Who today administers the various sections that were removed from the Minister of Agriculture? Subsequently the order in council of the 3rd of February was repealed on the 20th of February, but as yet we have had no information as to what actually took place during those 17 days. In particular, we want to be furnished with a record of all the directives and orders made by the Minister of Agriculture between those two dates in connection with the branches which were transferred to the Minister of Forestry.
The law in this connection is set forth in the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act, section 2 of which reads in part as follows:
The governor in council may
(a) transfer any powers, duties or functions or supervision of any part of the public service from one minister of the crown to any other minister of the crown, or from one department or portion of the public service to any other department or portion of the public service.
This transfer of powers is one of the most peculiar and unusual things that have taken place since I have been a member of the house. There have been transfers made before but never has there been such an element of mystery. One really does not know what went on. Never before was so much power bandied between so few to the detriment of the public service in general.
What we are trying to find out is who had the power. What happened? What were the circumstances under which this irresponsible game of transfer and retransfer took place? The committee will understand that there is a bit of mystery about this matter because the Minister of Forestry went to Vancouver and there he explained what had happened. We have not had that explanation here. He said, as reported in Le Devoir on March 25:
The department of forestry and rural development which the federal government is going to set up will be independent of the Department of Agriculture, Hon. Maurice Sauve, Minister of Forestry in the Pearson government said yesterday. The minister stated, "a brand new, autonomous department, with one or two deputy ministers, one for forests, the other for rural development" will be established.
I would ask this question. Is it a fact that as a result of the uncertainty in these two departments employees did not receive their pay in the regular way as they should have? I refer to the employees of the animal diseases research institute of the animal pathology division located on Gamelin boulevard in
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
Hull. Did they have to wait five weeks for their pay cheques and, if so, why? Was it because no one knew whether this matter came under the department of forestry and rural development, the latter part as yet unconstituted, or under the Department of Agriculture?
It is this information for which we ask, and naturally as soon as the information is received we will be able to go on to another department. There are some very important questions to be answered by the minister but the general questions that have been asked are still up in the air. So far all we have seen is fumbling attempts to field the questions on this problem. We have seen the shifting of powers over a period of days of indecision during which one minister or the other must have been in doubt as to which was in fact to discharge certain functions. It was a case of off again, on again. Taking the most charitable view that one can of this series of episodes, that view is that this is just another case of crossed wires in the cabinet, of faltering leadership, of disregard for proper, effective and decisive procedure.
It is these things we are anxious to find out about. This group of supplementary estimates involves a tremendous amount of money, a quarter of a billion dollars, and in addition we have this clumsy, ineffective and doubtful transfer of powers which after three weeks ended up leaving everybody where they were and with no one knowing who exercised the authority that had to be exercised during the period of uncertainty.
There are other matters I shall deal with later. The other day the minister made some references to the way things were going in agriculture. He also referred to the cattle situation. I feel he should give us information as to the prices of cattle in 1961, 1962, 1963 and during the first months of 1964 up to the present. It would also be very helpful if we had-he has all this information at his fingertips-information as to the number of cattle exported to the United States in 1961, 1962, 1963 and 1964 to date.
I am sure the minister is desirous of cooperating in every way and wishes to give the committee the benefit of his knowledge. If he will just answer these questions rather than rising and bumbling away on something we have not asked him about we will make progress. We have a great many important items to deal with which will require examination. There is one particularly large item about which I know he will want to give us the fullest information. Therefore, without further delay I leave the matter with him, knowing he will bring together in his own inimitable manner these threads of uncertainty, these threads of authority, some of

which have disappeared, others of which have been broken and some of which have been reassembled, so that order will be brought out of the chaos of two departments.

Mr. Chairman, with some of the things the Leader of the Opposition said both prior to five o'clock and since eight o'clock, we agree. We have already made it clear that we feel we are in the squeeze, to quote one of the Ottawa newspapers today, that we are now in because of the introduction of four days of the budget debate into a schedule that was already crowded. We think there are other examples of the mismanagement of the business of the house by the government, but they can be dealt with at some other time. We agree also that when supplementary estimates are before us they should be examined carefully. They should be scrutinized. We think this job should be done decently and properly. We should take whatever time is necessary, although we should not waste time.
However, Mr. Chairman, the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition in this house indulged in a display this afternoon that I cannot let pass without putting the record straight. I wondered for a time during the supper hour whether or not I would let it pass, but an editorial which I read during the supper hour in the Ottawa Journal made it clear this was something concerning which the record must be put straight. When he was speaking prior to five o'clock, the Leader of the Opposition stated categorically that the Minister of Justice tried to force this house to sit on Good Friday. Later, the Leader of the Opposition put on the record most of what was said at six o'clock on Thursday. If anyone reads carefully what was said at that time, it will be very clear that the Minister of Justice, far from trying to force this house to sit on Good Friday, was doing his best to help the house avoid sitting on Good Friday. I could raise it as a point of privilege because I, personally, am involved in the charges that were made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition.
I was pointing out we were informed at six o'clock last Tuesday that the motion to which I have already referred had been filed for the order paper. This was objected to by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. I did not share the reasons for his objections, but I joined with him in objecting. I suggested that it might be better if this motion were withdrawn rather than let it appear to be giving the house a threat. The Minister of Justice said, "What do we do about Good Friday; I want to be sure we do not sit on Good Friday." We all said, the representatives of all parties, "We can handle that by making sure that you will have unanimous consent not to sit on Good Friday. It is not necessary," we said to the Minister of Justice, "to have that kind of motion since it is going to seem to be a threat to some of the members of the house. If you withdraw the motion, we will undertake that you will have the unanimous consent that will be necessary so that the house will not have to sit on Good Friday."
The Minister of Justice, at that meeting at supper time last Tuesday, told us he would give consideration to our request and that he would carry on any consultations with his colleagues which might be necessary. We were invited to meet in his office at ten o'clock that same night. We went to his office at ten o'clock that night. To keep the record perfectly straight, I was a minute or two late getting there. As I got there, the meeting was breaking up. I had thought it might last an hour, but I was told the minister had informed us he had withdrawn the motion, so any need for a further meeting that night was avoided.
There is the story, Mr. Chairman; the motion to adjourn the house from Thursday night to Monday was withdrawn. The motion the Ottawa Journal said the government should have introduced was filed, but it was withdrawn at the request of representatives of the opposition, led in fact by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre; and I suggest in the light of that it is crystal clear- certainly it is clear beyond peradventure of doubt to me-that the Minister of Justice is the last man in the house to be accused of trying to force the house to sit on Good Friday.
We met several times after those meetings of last Tuesday, and on almost every occasion the question came up, what about Good

Friday? I admit the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said I might have some difficulty. In fact I admitted at the meeting that I might have difficulty with one or two of my members who might not want to give unanimous consent but I stated I would do my best, that I would take the matter up in our party caucus, and I later reported we had unanimous agreement in our caucus not to object to any motion necessary to avoid sitting on Good Friday. As late as the last meeting we had on Thursday I was able to say there would be no difficulty so far as we of the New Democratic party were concerned.
Certainly at those meetings of house leaders we had a number of disagreements about house business, but on this point there was no disagreement whatever. A sitting on Good Friday was to be avoided, and it was to be avoided by all parties undertaking that there would be unanimous consent to any motion necessary not to sit on Good Friday. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, last Thursday evening when I heard the Leader of the Opposition twisting the words of the Minister of Justice into a suggestion that we sit on Good Friday I could hardly believe my ears. I wondered if the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre had not been reporting to his leader what had taken place. Then a little later, as if my ears were not already hearing enough that I could not believe, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre himself said, "Now the present group are asking us to sit on Good Friday." I repeat that this came from the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre who was at the meeting of house leaders, who protested against this motion and at whose request the motion was withdrawn. So, in the light of that, to upbraid and criticize the Minister of Justice, as the Leader of the Opposition did this afternoon, is to accuse him of something which is the very opposite of what he tried to do for three or four days on end, and is a performance not worthy of the right hon. gentleman who was formerly prime minister of this country and who is now leader of the official opposition.
Now, I repeat, we have our difficulties. We had our difficulties about what we were to do before we adjourned, but there was no doubt in my mind about what the government was asking for-that the government was asking for both interim supply and supplementary estimates. The hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre would not accept this; he would not agree, but there was no doubt what the government wanted.
We had various other disagreements, and I still hold to the view that the government made a serious mistake when in the first place it brought down the budget. I think it has made a number of mistakes. In fact I am

keeping a list of them and some time when I have 40 minutes to speak I am going to read out its mistakes; but on this one issue of who was responsible for the house sitting on Good Friday the record itself is clear, and certainly the one person to whom no blame attaches for that sitting is the Minister of Justice. Nobody did more than he to try to avoid it, and I think the Leader of the Opposition, the Ottawa Journal and any others accusing him of this, owe him an apology.

I am pleased to be able to give an account of the supplementary estimates as far as the Department of Agriculture is concerned and I shall do my best to answer all the questions which have been asked in this connection. I have listed these questions, but there are matters I may have missed and, if I could be reminded of them, I will endeavour to answer those questions, too, to the satisfaction of the committee.
I think, first of all, X should make a short statement in reply to what was said by the Leader of the Opposition. There has been considerable discussion on this matter of the transfer of certain functions between myself and the Minister of Forestry. Some, probably wishfully, have attempted to imply that certain functions have been taken from me against my wishes. I would like to assure them that any such interpretation is entirely without foundation. X am in complete accord with the arrangements which have been made.
The government and I, as Minister of Agriculture, have only one goal in agricultural matters and that is to administer agricultural policies as soundly and progressively as possible in the interests of Canadian agriculture.
The Minister of Agriculture has a wide range of heavy responsibilities. He is responsible for the administration of over 30 statutes and a number of non-statutory policies through a department of around 10,000 employees. In addition, as the Prime Minister has announced, he is to be responsible for railway branch line rationalization. It is perfectly logical, and indeed desirable, that some responsibilities should be transferred to another minister who is conveniently able to carry them. This is the reason why ARDA, MMRA and feed grain policy have been transferred to the Minister of Forestry, and I
Supply-Agriculture
repeat that there was complete agreement between us on this.
The acts which remain with the Department of Agriculture are as follows: the Agricultural Products Board Act; the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act; the Agricultural Products Marketing Act; the Agricultural Stabilization Act; the Animal Contagious Diseases Act; the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act; the Canada Dairy Products Act; the Canada Grain Act; the Cheese and Cheese Factory Improvement Act; the Cold Storage Act; the Crop Insurance Act; the Department of Agriculture Act; the Destructive Insect and Pest Act; the Experimental Farm Stations Act; the Farm Credit Act; the Feeds Act; the Fertilizers Act; the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act; the Hay and Straw Inspection Act; the Humane Slaughter of Food Animals Act; the Inspection and Sale Act; the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act; the Live Stock Pedigree Act; the Maple Products Industry Act; the Meat and Canned Foods Act; the Meat Inspection Act; the Milk Test Act; the Pest Control Products Act; the Prairie Farm Assistance Act; the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act; the Seeds Act; the Wheat Co-operative Marketing Act; and the Criminal Code, section 178, race track betting. So hon. members can see I have not been stripped of all of my acts.
There seems to be some effort to create the impression that the powers of the Minister of Agriculture are gradually being whittled away. In the debate on supplementary estimates on March 13 the right hon. Leader of the Opposition referred to responsibility for the Canadian wheat board having been taken earlier from the Minister of Agriculture. Presumably he considers this wrong, or a reflection on the Minister of Agriculture, that the wheat board should be under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Well, he was the head of the government from June, 1957 onward yet it was not until October of 1960 that the wheat board was placed under the minister of agriculture. Are we to interpret it as a reflection on the then minister of trade and commerce that the wheat board was taken from him at that time? Or, if the wheat board is considered to be a proper responsibility of the Minister of Agriculture, why was there a delay of three years before action was taken at that time? In fact, it is by no means an improper arrangement for certain measures such as the ARDA program to be placed with another minister whose interests and other responsibilities are clearly associated with them.
I would point out, as has been stated by the Acting Prime Minister, that there is to be a three man executive committee to co-ordinate policies for agriculture. It is to consist of the

Supply-Agriculture
Minister of Agriculture as chairman and the ministers of trade and commerce and forestry. No one need have any fear that there will not be full co-ordination between the different ministers and departments having responsibility for agricultural matters.
I have had some experience in working with both private and public bodies. I have never been associated with any group in which there was better team-work than there is in the government of which I am proud to be a member.
Mr. Chairman, the first hon. member who spoke as far as my estimates are concerned had something to say about calf hides and cow hides and their price. Of course, this does not come under my department but I can honestly say that I realize this is a great problem to the people who have stored many of these hides, some of them for years. As a matter of fact several people who have thousands of hides in store have come to see me and they have been to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce. There is a serious world problem in so far as hides are concerned. This year so far-and this answers another question-we have exported something like 175,000 head of cattle. Our exports generally run as high as 500,000 head. We are very fortunate in Canada vis-a-vis the situation that existed in the United States when they had a great surplus of cattle. They had been importing something over one million head from Australia; they were bringing in almost the same number from Mexico. This was causing them great concern. Twelve per cent of their beef was being imported, and they were moving to do something about this. They put on certain quotas; that is, red meat quotas in so far as beef cattle are concerned. This is the situation in the United States, and it does not affect Canada. I think they were very careful not to disturb the Canadian position. However, we found ourselves in the position where we had to slaughter something like 300,000 more head of cattle in the year than we generally have to slaughter in Canada. This gave us, not a matter of 6,000 or 7,000 more hides, but many thousands more hides, and we were already having a marketing problem. Hides have been substituted by plastics and this sort of thing, and I think we are going to have some difficulty in so far as hides are concerned for quite some time until possibly there is a new market or a new use found for hides.
I was also asked the question about prices of cattle. I realize that prices of cattle are not as high as they have been in the past, but I partly explained why this is so. The price of our cattle in Canada today is higher than that of United States cattle. This has

not been the situation for many, many years. In other words, when our slaughterings of reds and blues-which are quality cattle in Canada-reached, say 18,000 heads, we would generally go on the export market and would move our cattle across the line into the United States market. It was not possible to do that this year. If we had been able to move them across into the United States, our live cattle today would have been possibly 16 cents or 17 cents a pound. In other words, our cattle must be 5 cents per pound higher than American cattle before American cattle can start to move into Canada.
Since June 15 this year we have consumed more beef per capita than we have for many, many years. It would look as though we are consuming at the rate of about 81 pounds of meat per capita. I humbly suggest to the committee that there is only one reason for our consuming this amount of beef, and that is because of our buoyant economy. People who work are people who buy our meat, and if we had not had a decline in unemployment it would have hurt not only the beef producers but most of our agricultural products. This is the situation that exists in so far as hides are concerned.
Another question one hon. member asked me was in connection with feed grain. A great deal was said today about agricultural policy. In so far as our feed grain is concerned, on August 27 we changed the policy, or whatever you wish to call it. I think the feed grain act started in 1941, whereby the federal government provided freight assistance from the great lakes to eastern spots in so far as western grain is concerned. Due to the tremendous sales of wheat and the amount of wheat that might have to move to seaboard, both to the Pacific coast and to the eastern coast, a great many consumers of feed grain were terrifically worried about their position so far as feed grain was concerned. This was a reasonable attitude for them to take.
We knew as early as the middle of August that there would probably be some difficulty in getting this feed to eastern spots. Therefore we decided to pay not only the freight rate but also the storage charges on grain from October 15 to April 15 in order that we might not only stop the speculation by the people supplying this grain to the producer, but also to help stabilize the price. If a buyer from Granby wanted to buy grain that was coming from western Canada, they could buy it and pay for it when they saw fit at any time before they were to sell the grain to the eastern farmer. This also helped to stabilize the grain situation in so far as feed grains are concerned. This policy did even more than we expected it might do. We thought that

toward the end of navigation we would have enough grain located in eastern Canada and would not have to bring any down by rail. As at last week we had 47 per cent more grain, or something like 21 million more bushels, on spot in eastern Canada and it will not be necessary to bring any by rail to eastern Canada.
There was some mention of the price of grain now at eastern spots. I am happy to report that, although wheat is somewhat up, No. 1 feed barley is $4.38 a ton less than it was a year ago; No. 1 feed oats are $2.50 a ton less than they were a year ago; and Ontario corn is $1.08 less than it was a year ago. As I said, we do have on spot ample grain to take care of the requirements of the feeder in eastern Canada, and this is the first time for many, many years that this has been possible. This is coupled with the fact that we have shipped more grain out of Canada from both east coast and west coast and have had a record year in this connection.
What is the stability of the grain that was moved into eastern spots? In Quebec, in December, the cost of No. 1 feed oats was $2.43 per cwt. and in March it is $2.46, or 3 cents difference, which is a very small amount. Feed barley was $2.40 per cwt. in December, and in March $2.44. In Montreal, in December, oats were $2.48, and in March $2.49. In so far as barley is concerned, in December it was $2.39, and in March $2.43. So we feel that this policy of paying the storage and the freight, has helped stabilize the situation and has also helped us to gather ample amounts of grain in eastern locations for the eastern farmer. I am sure that if hon. members go out in the country, as we have done on many occasions, and ask the farmers, these farmers will assure them that this situation although it may not be perfect, has certainly effected some improvement. We hope that next year we will be able to improve it even more, and I am sure this is also the wish of every member of this house.
In so far as dairy policy is concerned, my hon. friend from St. Hyacinthe-Bagot spoke yesterday about this matter. Hon. members will remember that on May 1, 1963 we did change the dairy policy and took the subsidy off fluid milk, but we did put a premium on cheese. I telephoned yesterday to get the price of milk at Granby and St. Hyacinthe. In 1963 uncooled milk was $2.85 per cwt., cooled milk was $2.95 and bulk tank milk was $3.00. In 1964 uncooled milk was $2.95, 10 cents higher in the constituency of the hon. member than it was in 1963. Cooled milk was $3.05 per cwt., 10 cents higher, and bulk milk was $3.10, again 10 cents higher. I think this condition has existed all over Canada.
Royal Assent
Now perhaps I might say a few words about butter. We have been storing butter since 1957 because of the very high support required, 64 cents a pound butterfat. In 1963 we changed our dairy policy and put a premium on cheese milk. The thinking was that if we did this it would result in larger cheese production, and we had a market for all our cheese. I do not know the exact figures but it seems to me that the Canadian producers converted more milk from butter to cheese, which resulted in 18 million pounds more cheese being produced, compared with the previous year, and cheese for which we had a market. I realize we have more cheese in store today, but this does not concern us as much as being able to level off the consumption and production of butter.
Then I was asked what we were doing about exporting butter to Great Britain. I made an announcement some time ago in this house, I think in early fall, that we had decided that the time had come when we should start to move some of our butter stock. We had been able to level off production and consumption, and it was costing us $350,000 a month storage, so we decided it would be better to take a loss and to move this butter into a market if possible. I am pleased to report that we have been able to move some of this butter. In moving it into Great Britain we first had to get the permission of the quota countries sending butter to Britain, and they allowed us to send five million pounds. I also think we supplied them with 4-J million pounds of butter oil.

I have the honour to inform the house that I have received the following communication:
Government House, Ottawa, March 30, 1964
Sir:
I have the honour to inform you that the Honourable Wishart F. Spence, puisne Judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, acting as Deputy to His Excellency the Governor General, will proceed to the Senate chamber today, 30th March, at 9.45 p.m., for the purpose of giving the royal assent to certain bills.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
A. G. Cherrier
Assistant Secretary to the Governor General

Royal Assent
A message was delivered by Major C. R. Lamoureux, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Honourable the Deputy Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable house in the chamber of the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker with the house went up to the Senate chamber.
And being returned:
Mr. Speaker informed the house that the Deputy Governor General has been pleased to give, in Her Majesty's name, the royal assent to the following bills:
An act respecting the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act.
An act for granting to Her Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending the 31st March, 1965.
It being 16 minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.
